title: Services & EndpointSlices
summary: Give a changing set of Pods one stable address: selectors, Service types, ports, headless Services, EndpointSlices and discovery.

blocks.text: Bays come and go, and their phone numbers change. So each job gets a **fixed port phone number** (a Service) that forwards to whichever bays currently do it. It finds them by coloured tag (the selector), and the switchboard's list of bays (EndpointSlices) stays current automatically. Callers dial the Service's `port`, which rings the bay's own line (`targetPort`), even by line name, so bays can renumber without breaking callers. Unless you say otherwise, it's an internal extension (ClusterIP).

Pods are ephemeral and their IPs change. A **Service** puts one stable address in front of a group of Pods. Its **selector** picks the Pods by label, and a controller keeps the Service's **EndpointSlices** in sync with the matching Pods.

blocks.title: A Service in front of its Pods

steps.text: A **Service** selects Pods by label. `app=web` matches two Pods; the `app=api` Pod isn't selected.
Clients use the Service's stable virtual IP or DNS name instead of individual Pod IPs.
The control plane keeps the matching Pod addresses in **EndpointSlices** and updates them as Pods come and go.
Requests are spread across the ready backend Pods.

blocks.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: <service-name>
spec:
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: <app-label>
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: <service-port>
      targetPort: <container-port>

items: No `type` means the default, **ClusterIP**.
If you leave out `targetPort`, it defaults to the value of `port`.
`targetPort` can be a **port name** defined in the Pod (for example `http-web-svc`), so backends can change port numbers without breaking clients.
Default protocol is **TCP**.
With **multiple ports**, every port must have a name (lowercase alphanumerics and `-`, starting and ending with an alphanumeric).

blocks.text: Port numbers come in four kinds. An **internal extension** (ClusterIP) works only inside the port. A **numbered gate on every ship** (NodePort, 30000-32767 by default) adds outside access through the same gate number everywhere. A **public entrance the city builds** (LoadBalancer) adds an outside balancer that the liaison to the city points at those gates. A **forwarding note** (ExternalName) just tells callers another hostname, with no switchboard involved.

rows: Cluster-internal virtual IP; reachable only inside the cluster
ClusterIP **plus** the same static port opened on every node
NodePort **plus** an external load balancer (from a cloud provider or one you provide)
DNS **CNAME** to the `externalName` hostname; no proxying

items: NodePort ports come from `--service-node-port-range`, **default 30000-32767**. The port is shown in `.spec.ports[*].nodePort`; you can request one with `nodePort`.
For LoadBalancer, the cloud-controller-manager points the external balancer at the node port. Details appear in `.status.loadBalancer`.
Set `spec.allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false` to skip node ports (only if the balancer routes straight to Pods).
You can pick a specific `.spec.clusterIP`; it must lie inside `service-cluster-ip-range`, or the API server returns 422.
ExternalName expects a hostname. A value that looks like an IPv4 address isn't resolved. HTTP and TLS can break because the hostname differs.

blocks.text: Three numbers, three places. The **port** is the extension callers dial on the Service itself. The **targetPort** is the line inside the bay where the call finally rings, given as a number or a named line. The **nodePort** is the gate number opened on every ship for NodePort and LoadBalancer Services. Mixing them up is like giving a visitor standing at the ship's gate the bay's internal line instead of the gate number.

rows: The port the Service listens on (with its ClusterIP)
The Pod port traffic goes to; a number or a named `containerPort`
The port opened on every node for NodePort/LoadBalancer

blocks.text:
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: <app-label>
  ports:
    - port: <service-port>
      targetPort: <container-port>
      nodePort: <port-in-30000-32767>

Sometimes callers want the bays themselves, not a switchboard. A **headless** number (`clusterIP: None`) has no extension of its own, so the switchboard ignores it and the directory hands back each bay's own number. A number with **no selector** gets no automatic bay list; you write the list yourself and tag it `kubernetes.io/service-name`, handy for an outside database. Those hand-written entries can't be loopback numbers or another Service's extension.

**Headless:** set `.spec.clusterIP: None`. No cluster IP is allocated, kube-proxy ignores the Service and nothing is load-balanced. DNS returns the **Pod IPs** directly (A/AAAA records). `None` is not the same as leaving the field empty.

**No selector:** Kubernetes creates no EndpointSlices. Add one yourself and link it with the `kubernetes.io/service-name: <service-name>` label. Useful for an external database or a backend in another namespace or cluster.
Manual endpoint IPs can't be loopback, link-local, or another Service's cluster IP. `kubectl port-forward` to a selectorless Service fails.

Behind each port number, the switchboard keeps **cards** listing the current bays (EndpointSlices). Supervisors write them automatically for numbers with a selector, at most 100 bays per card by default, with IPv4 and IPv6 on separate cards. Each entry notes the bay's ship and zone, and whether it is ready, serving or terminating. The switchboard operator (`kube-proxy`) trusts these cards as the source of truth. They replace the older single-sheet Endpoints list.

items: The control plane creates EndpointSlices automatically for every Service **with a selector**.
They are linked to their Service by the `kubernetes.io/service-name` label and an owner reference.
Default limit is **100 endpoints per slice**, changeable with the kube-controller-manager flag `--max-endpoints-per-slice` (max 1000).
IPv4 and IPv6 go in separate slices, so a dual-stack Service has at least two.
Each endpoint carries `nodeName` and `zone`, plus conditions: **ready**, **serving**, **terminating**.
`ready` is roughly "serving and not terminating". For Pods, `serving` follows the Pod's Ready condition.
kube-proxy uses EndpointSlices as its **source of truth** for routing.
Slices managed by the controller have `endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by: endpointslice-controller.k8s.io`.
They replace the older **Endpoints** API; mirroring Endpoints into slices is deprecated since v1.33.

blocks.text: The quickest way to get a port number is to point at an existing contract or bay and say "give that a number" (`kubectl expose`). The clerk copies its coloured-tag selector, picks an internal extension unless you ask for another `--type`, and can copy the port too. `--cluster-ip=None` makes it headless. Add `--dry-run=client -o yaml` to get the paperwork as a draft you can edit, for example to fix the gate number.
Creates a Service by copying the **selector** of an existing pod, service, replicationcontroller, deployment or replicaset.

kubectl expose deployment <name> --port=<service-port> --target-port=<container-port>
kubectl expose pod <pod-name> --port=<service-port> --name=<service-name>
kubectl expose deployment <name> --port=<service-port> --type=NodePort

items: `--type`: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer or ExternalName. **Default ClusterIP.**
`--port` is copied from the resource if you leave it out.
`--cluster-ip=None` creates a headless Service.
A Deployment or ReplicaSet can be exposed only if its selector uses `matchLabels` alone.

blocks.text: `kubectl expose` is the fastest way to create a Service. Add `--dry-run=client -o yaml` to get a manifest you can edit, for example to set a fixed `nodePort`.

sections.heading: Finding a Service: env vars and DNS

blocks.text: How does a bay learn a port number? When a bay opens, the cargo officer pins a **printed list** of active numbers inside (environment variables like `{SVCNAME}_SERVICE_HOST`), but numbers created later never make that list. The **port phone directory** (cluster DNS such as CoreDNS) has no such gap: ask for `<service>` in your own yard, or `<service>.<ns>` from anywhere. Forwarding notes (ExternalName) can only be found through the directory.

items: **Environment variables:** the kubelet adds `{SVCNAME}_SERVICE_HOST` and `{SVCNAME}_SERVICE_PORT` for each active Service (name upper-cased, dashes become underscores).
Env vars are only set if the Service **existed before** the Pod started. DNS has no such ordering problem.
**DNS:** with a cluster DNS add-on such as CoreDNS, a Service `<service>` in namespace `<ns>` resolves as `<service>` from the same namespace and `<service>.<ns>` from anywhere.
Named ports get **SRV** records, for example `_http._tcp.<service>.<ns>`.
ExternalName Services can only be reached through DNS.

questions.stem: A Service manifest has no type field. Which type is it?

options.explanation: ClusterIP is the default type.
NodePort has to be set explicitly.
LoadBalancer has to be set explicitly.
Headless isn't a type; it's clusterIP: None.

questions.stem: Pods listen on TCP 9376. Clients inside the cluster should connect to the Service on port 80. Which ports block is right?

options.explanation: port is what the Service exposes; targetPort is the Pod's port.
This is reversed: it would send traffic to Pod port 80.
nodePort is a node-level port from the NodePort range, not the Pod port.
targetPort would default to 80, but the Pods listen on 9376.

questions.stem: With the default settings, which nodePort value can you request?

options.explanation: It falls inside the default range 30000-32767.
Outside the default NodePort range.
Outside the default NodePort range.
Outside the default NodePort range.

questions.stem: Which statements about a type: LoadBalancer Service are true by default? Select 2.

options.text: It also gets a cluster IP and node ports
options.explanation: Types are nested: LoadBalancer builds on NodePort, which builds on ClusterIP.

options.text: The provisioned balancer is reported in .status.loadBalancer
options.explanation: Creation is asynchronous; details land in the status.

options.text: Kubernetes ships its own load balancer component
options.explanation: You must provide one or integrate with a cloud provider.
allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts defaults to true.

questions.stem: Your app should reach an external database by a stable in-cluster name. The database has a DNS hostname. Which Service type fits?

options.explanation: It maps the Service to a DNS name with a CNAME record.
NodePort exposes in-cluster Pods on node ports.
LoadBalancer exposes in-cluster Pods externally.

questions.stem: For a headless Service (clusterIP: None), kube-proxy load-balances traffic across the Pods.

options.explanation: kube-proxy does not handle headless Services.
Correct. DNS returns the Pod IPs and clients connect directly.

questions.stem: You create a Service with no selector for an external backend. Traffic goes nowhere. What is missing?

options.text: An EndpointSlice you create yourself, labelled kubernetes.io/service-name with the Service name
options.explanation: Without a selector, no EndpointSlices are created automatically.
The type doesn't create endpoints.
That makes it headless but still gives no endpoints.
kube-proxy has no endpoints to route to.

questions.stem: How many endpoints does an EndpointSlice hold at most, by default?

options.explanation: The default; configurable up to 1000.
1000 is the maximum you can configure, not the default.
The default is 100.
The default limit is 100.

questions.stem: Which are conditions stored on EndpointSlice endpoints? Select 3.

options.explanation: One of the three conditions.
One of the three conditions.
One of the three conditions.
Not one of the three conditions EndpointSlices store.

questions.stem: A dual-stack Service has at least two EndpointSlices: one for IPv4 and one for IPv6.

options.explanation: Each EndpointSlice holds one address type.
Each slice is a single address type, so dual-stack needs two or more.

questions.stem: Which command creates a Service on port 80 for Deployment nginx whose containers listen on 8000?

options.explanation: --port is the Service port; --target-port is the container port.
The ports are reversed.
--protocol sets TCP, UDP or SCTP, not a port.
--name sets the Service name.

questions.stem: Which kubectl expose flag value creates a headless Service?

options.explanation: Setting the cluster IP to None makes the Service headless.
That creates an ExternalName Service.
--external-ip adds an extra external IP to accept.

questions.stem: A client Pod's code reads MY_DB_SERVICE_HOST, but the variable is missing. The my-db Service exists. What is the likely cause?

options.text: The client Pod was created before the Service
options.explanation: Service env vars are only injected for Services that exist when the Pod starts.

options.text: Env vars only work for headless Services
options.explanation: The kubelet injects them for each active Service.

options.text: The variable should be named MY-DB_SERVICE_HOST
options.explanation: Dashes are converted to underscores.
Env vars are injected by the kubelet, not by DNS.

questions.stem: A Pod outside namespace my-ns must reach Service my-service in my-ns. Which name works?

options.explanation: Pods in other namespaces must qualify the name with the namespace.
The short name only works from the Service's own namespace.
The Service name comes first, then the namespace.

questions.stem: Expose the Deployment `nginx` as a Service on port 80 that forwards to container port 8000.
questions.explanation: `--port` is the Service's port; `--target-port` is the port on the Pods traffic is sent to.
